milestones.title: Milestone and DAG driven development
milestones.problem: Work in this repository was planned in conversation and in task records that describe one session at a time. There was no executable specification of an outcome, no dependency graph between pieces of work, and no way for a fresh worker to ask the repository what to do next. The tool supervises a task; nothing supervised the plan the task belonged to.
milestones.outcome: Every non-trivial change in this repository belongs to a milestone specification and to one dependency-linked issue execution contract, validated as a DAG, with status derived rather than asserted, and projected to GitHub and to the website from that one canonical model.
milestones.current_state: The canonical model, its engine, its CLI, its projections, its doctrines and its tests exist and are exercised by this milestone's own issues. GitHub carried no issues and no milestones before this work.
milestones.desired_state: A fresh worker with no conversation history runs `majordomus plan next`, receives one issue, executes it inside its declared scope, attaches evidence, and the graph recomputes what is ready without anybody editing a status field.
non_scope: A hosted planning backend or database
A second project-management vocabulary; milestones and issues are the only new nouns
Bidirectional GitHub write-back into the canonical files
Estimation, burndown, velocity or any scheduling model
acceptance_criteria: The canonical model parses, rejects unknown keys, and refuses a duplicate id
A dependency cycle, a self-dependency and an unknown dependency are each rejected with a named finding
READY, BLOCKED, ACTIVE, VERIFY, DONE and CANCELLED are derived from recorded facts and stored nowhere
Execution waves are computed from the graph, and overlapping scope inside one wave is reported
The Mermaid DAG is generated from the same graph the CLI reads
GitHub milestones and issues are created and updated from the canonical model, and drift between them is reported
The website renders the roadmap, every milestone, every issue and the DAG from generated data
Every surface agrees: the CLI, the site data and the GitHub projection report the same issue set and the same READY set
Changing one dependency changes every surface
CI refuses a push whose canonical model is invalid or whose generated artifacts are stale
risks: The engine is shell and awk; a graph large enough to make that slow would need a different implementation. Measured, not assumed.
GitHub is a projection. If a human edits a generated issue body, the next sync reports drift rather than silently overwriting it, which means drift can accumulate unattended.

evidence.result: every case in test/cases passed and none failed, each in a disposable repository
1 passed — the CLI, the JSON output, the Mermaid diagram, the GitHub projection and a freshly generated site-data file agree on every set they can be asked about
1 passed — every canonical mutation the case makes moves every surface
every milestone and issue the model held at this commit existed on korczis/prismatic-majordomus with its state matching the derived status; check exited 0 with no drift

milestones.title: A blocking question survives a handover
milestones.problem: An open question is the mechanism for stopping acceptance when work depends on a person. It is attached to the task that opened it, and the gate only reads questions belonging to the active task. Handing over and starting a new task therefore leaves the question unresolved and no longer blocking anything, so the one thing that was supposed to refuse a completed finish refuses nothing. The gap was found by running the documented end-to-end sequence, not by review, and it is published as a planned claim with no implementation and no test.
milestones.outcome: An unresolved question keeps refusing a completed finish after the work moves to a new task, or the alternative is chosen deliberately and the reason is recorded where the next worker will read it.
milestones.current_state: docs/CLAIMS.yaml carries blocker-survives-handover as planned, with implementation and test both '-'. lib/question.sh matches unresolved lines by the active task id; lib/check.sh reads only those. Nothing detects that a handover has orphaned a blocker.
milestones.desired_state: The behaviour is decided between two named alternatives, implemented, proved by a behavioural case, and the claim moves from planned to guaranteed with its implementation and test filled in.
non_scope: A question that blocks across repositories or worktrees
Assigning a question to a person, or notifying anybody
Any change to the finish contract's other lines
acceptance_criteria: A behavioural case demonstrates the current escape, so the gap is executable rather than asserted
The choice between transferring the question and widening the gate is recorded as a decision with what was rejected and why
The chosen behaviour is implemented and a case fails when it is removed
The claim in docs/CLAIMS.yaml moves to guaranteed with a real implementation path and a real test path
The claim detail page states what the behaviour does not cover
risks: Transferring a question with a handover makes it a property of the work rather than of the task, which is right in the common case and wrong when the handover is to a different piece of work. Widening the gate to every unresolved question blocks tasks that never opened one. The decision has to name the case it is choosing to be wrong in.

evidence.result: the case runs the documented sequence and the mutation section reproduces the escape from a probe that narrows the gate back to the active task, so the gap is executable rather than described
the choice, both rejected alternatives with the case each gets wrong, and the two conditions the choice imposed on the implementation

milestones.title: A durable record names the worker that wrote it
milestones.problem: Every durable record is attributed to the task that is active in the checkout, because decision, checkpoint and question all read .majordomus/state/current.yaml to find out whose work they belong to. Several workers share one checkout, so the record names whoever started a task there rather than whoever ran the command. In one evening three sessions wrote under another session's active task, and one decision had to be dropped by hand after the fact because the premise it recorded belonged to somebody else. Attribution is the one property of a record that cannot be reconstructed later: the conversation that would settle it is gone.
milestones.outcome: A durable record either names the worker that produced it or is refused, and a record written from one session can never arrive attributed to another session's task.
milestones.current_state: Not started. lib/decision.sh, lib/checkpoint.sh and lib/question.sh each resolve the active task from the checkout and write it into the record. Nothing distinguishes two workers sharing that checkout, and nothing reports that it cannot.
milestones.desired_state: Attribution is verifiable from the record alone. Where the tool cannot establish who wrote something, it says so and refuses rather than guessing from what happens to be active.
non_scope: A registry of named workers, personas or agents
Any identity the repository has to maintain, or that outlives the session that used it
Locking a checkout to one worker
acceptance_criteria: A record written while another worker's task is active is attributed correctly or refused by name
The attribution can be checked from the record alone, with no conversation history
No new record type and no registry of workers is introduced
A behavioural case reproduces two workers writing in one checkout
risks: The obvious fix is an identity the tool maintains, which is a registry of named workers by another name and is refused everywhere else in this repository. Whatever is chosen has to be supplied by the session and stored only inside the record it explains.
Refusing to write an unattributable record can lose a decision somebody was trying to make. The refusal has to say what to run instead, in the same breath.

milestones.title: A session is a durable envelope, and knowledge is compiled from what is already canonical
milestones.problem: Continuity today is task-shaped. A task record says what one piece of work is, and checkpoints, handovers, decisions and questions hang off it. Nothing represents the execution episode itself — the worker sat down, touched three tasks, recorded two decisions, closed one issue, and stopped — so the causal question a later worker actually asks is unanswerable from the records: which work happened together, in what order, against which commits, and what did it decide. The second gap is retrieval. `search` is a literal scan over six operational record kinds, which is right for those files and blind to everything else: the claims matrix, the milestone and issue contracts, the policy, the profiles, the prompts and the documents already carry explicit, machine-readable relationships — claim to implementation to test, issue to milestone to dependency, evidence to issue — and no command can traverse one of them. A worker therefore reconstructs both from a conversation, which is the thing that does not survive.
milestones.outcome: A worker with no conversation history can answer what happened, why, what was decided, which evidence supports it, where the canonical source lives, and what to do next — from records and a derived index, with git still the authority over both.
milestones.current_state: There is no session concept: `.majordomus/state/` holds task, checkpoint, handover, decision, question and ledger, and the ledger is the only thing that knows two records were written by the same episode, which it knows only by adjacency in time. There is no index of any kind; docs/CONTINUITY.md states that as a deliberate choice for the record corpus and says nothing about the rest of the repository. docs/DESIGN.md's Clean Extraction Boundary excludes graph semantics absolutely, which forbids even a provenance graph derived from this repository's own files.
milestones.desired_state: A session lifecycle exists with one active session per worktree and immutable closed records that reference authoritative records rather than copying them, and whose whole reference envelope is derived from the ledger instead of accumulated by hand. A knowledge compiler discovers curated sources through git, extracts nodes with identities that survive a rebuild, records edges only where an explicit relationship was observed, keeps a content-hash manifest that makes a no-op sync cheap, and answers read-only queries without mutating anything. `context` can select a bounded slice of it. Both are declared doctrines with validators that doctor and watch dispatch, and the boundary between shared and operational knowledge is a tested property rather than a convention.
non_scope: Any database, embedding, vector store, or similarity ranking
Any model invocation, network call, or generated summary
A second mutable narrative store that copies decisions, questions or checkpoint bodies
Publishing operational records to the website
Renderer-specific knowledge output for any particular note-taking application
Inferring a relationship from prose that does not state it explicitly
acceptance_criteria: A session opens, closes, and its closed record is immutable, temporally ordered, and interpretable against current git through the existing divergence vocabulary
A closed session names the tasks, issues, checkpoints, handovers, decisions and questions of its episode by reference, and copies none of their bodies
Knowledge discovery is driven by git rather than by a filesystem walk, and an untracked file is not a source
A node identity survives a rebuild, and editing one source changes only the nodes derived from it
Every edge carries the file it was observed in; an edge without provenance is a validation failure
A second sync with no source change reports no work and is measurably cheaper than a cold one
Every read-only knowledge and session command leaves `git status` byte-identical
Shared and operational knowledge are separable, and a test proves the shared projection contains no operational record
`context` can carry a bounded knowledge section that is dropped before any immutable fact and is named under EXCLUDED when it is
Each new guarantee is a declared doctrine with a validator that doctor and watch dispatch, a claim, and a behavioural case
docs/CONTINUITY.md and docs/DESIGN.md state the new architecture precisely instead of contradicting it
risks: A knowledge index is a second thing that can be believed. Every mitigation is the same one: the index is a pointer, it carries the source path and hash of what it points at, and it is reported stale rather than silently rebuilt by a query.

A curated source list is a place where something can be forgotten. The alternative — indexing everything git tracks — imports generated files, vendored trees and site output, and was rejected; the cost is that adding a canonical file kind is an explicit edit, and the validator names a declared source class whose discovery returns nothing.

Deriving a session's references from the ledger makes the ledger load-bearing for a second thing. It is already append-only, machine-written and validated by majordomus.ledger-integrity, and the alternative — accumulating references into a mutable session file on every command — puts a write on the hot path of every other command and creates the second store this milestone exists to avoid.

The Clean Extraction Boundary currently forbids graph semantics without qualification. Narrowing it is a deliberate change to a published boundary, and it must be narrowed precisely — a generic provenance graph over this repository's own artifacts — or it stops being a boundary.

milestones.title: Performance is executable evidence, and the hot path does no canonical work twice
milestones.problem: The shell tool is slow enough to be avoided: doctor takes ten seconds and runs on every commit through the pre-commit hook, watch takes the same, knowledge nodes six seconds, plan validate four, the site-data check and a single test case half a minute, and the suite half an hour. Nobody could say which phase paid for it, because nothing measured phases; the two validators that cost two thirds of doctor are loops of one awk process per key over files that were already flattened once. The Rust executable measured at the same time is fast, so the slowness is the shell tool's own.
milestones.outcome: Every public command can be benchmarked from the command registry with cold and warm distributions, the phases and work counters of any run can be printed, the caches and batch reads that remove repeated work preserve every observable result, an accepted baseline lives in the repository and a check refuses a regression by policy, and the pre-commit hook is fast enough that nobody routes around it.
milestones.current_state: MJ_TIMING prints per-validator phases and two work counters (feature/performance-truth 77f5d79). No benchmark command, no baseline, no regression check, no parse cache, no performance doctrine; the numbers above are the measured baseline on this repository.
milestones.desired_state: majordomus bench derives its targets from share/commands.yaml, records p50, p90, p95, p99, min, max, mean and stddev per command and mode, persists local runs under .ai/local/benchmarks/, compares against .ai/repo/benchmarks/baseline.json under the policy's benchmark block, and exits non-zero on a regression. Registry, catalogue, project-model and coverage validators read each flat file once. Flattened YAML is cached under .ai/local/cache/ by content hash. Project rules state the doctrine, docs/PERFORMANCE.md explains it, and CI runs the structural checks.
non_scope: Any change to apps/majordomus-cli, whose measured latency is not the problem
A metrics database, a dashboard, a tracing backend or any telemetry service
Hot reload or filesystem watching
A persistent capability result cache across processes beyond the flatten cache
Benchmarking external services
acceptance_criteria: Every public command in share/commands.yaml is a benchmark target without a second list anywhere
Cold and warm distributions are recorded separately with p50, p95 and p99 and never mixed
A local run is persisted under .ai/local/benchmarks/ and never treated as a baseline
The committed baseline is updated only by an explicit command on a clean tree
bench --check exits non-zero on a regression over the policy thresholds and names the command, the metric, both values and the threshold
Every canonical file is flattened at most once per command, proved by the work counters in a case
A cache hit and a cache miss produce byte-identical command output for every read-only command, proved by a case
doctor on this repository runs under the budget the policy declares, and the pre-commit hook inherits it
The performance rules are project rules under .ai/repo/rules/project, and docs/PERFORMANCE.md is the reference the README points at
risks: A cache is a second thing that can be believed. The flatten cache is keyed by the content hash of the file it caches, so a stale entry cannot be read for a changed file; it can only cost a miss.
Wall-clock thresholds are noisy across machines. The regression policy is conservative and relative, the structural counters are exact, and only the counters gate CI strictly.
Batching reads changes how validators are written. Each rewrite is proved by the case that already exists for the validator, run before and after, plus the counter case.

milestones.title: An adopting repository survives a Majordomus upgrade, and what the tool vendors into it is adopter-neutral
milestones.problem: A downstream repository, OSCILLA, audited on 2026-10-04 against v0.13.0 (e08aec8651), shows the tool breaking its adopters in ways no test in this repository sees, because every test here runs this repository's own layout. Installing 0.12.0 machine-wide made doctor report 433 failures in OSCILLA: unsealed plan stamps and use-case steps reclassified as state-mutating. Its pre-commit hook runs doctor, so every commit was refused until the layer was migrated by hand, and the migrated layer is then rejected by 0.10. Nothing records which tool version a layer was written for, and migrate handles only .majordomus to .ai. Live use-case scenarios refuse read-only knowledge subcommands while admitting check --checkpoint, which writes. Upgrading the vendored rules leaves the policy and source keys they depend on behind. The knowledge deriver writes untracked candidates onto a trunk that only pull requests change. The vendored rules and the init skeleton carry this repository's narrative, test paths and stack.
milestones.outcome: An adopter can upgrade the tool, or vendor its rules, and be told exactly what to migrate before anything refuses its commits. The migration is a command, not a hand replay. What the tool writes into an adopter (rules, skeleton, scope, candidates) is neutral to this repository and keeps a PR-only trunk clean.
milestones.current_state: At e08aec8651 the manifest and policy name no tool or layer version. SEALED_FROM is one global constant (lib/project.awk:45, plan.rs:122). share/commands.yaml classes each top-level command once. lib/migrate.sh moves only .majordomus/. docs/INSTALL.md says only to re-run the installer to upgrade. The knowledge deriver writes .ai/repo/knowledge/candidates/ in whichever checkout closes an episode. The rule package manifest says source_revision 0.6.0.
milestones.desired_state: doctor separates version-skew findings from defects and names the migration that clears them. migrate carries a layer from one version to the next, including re-sealing old plan stamps with their original times. The effect class is judged per subcommand and flag. rules vendor update reports or applies the skeleton keys the new rules need. Candidates never dirty a trunk. Vendored rules and the init skeleton say nothing that is only true of this repository.

Others are not. The full scheduled CI plan, the only one that selects every gate, has not produced a green verdict in its last 10 runs while push runs on master stay green, and nothing alarms; rule project.never-reported-is-not-green is review-only. rule-proof calls a rule satisfied when its proof is named and present: of 163 rules, 133 are 'not run'. milestones.title: Repository automation is scripted capabilities over typed Rust, not shell
milestones.problem: Repository automation lives in shell, and every recurring defect class this repository has recorded about itself has a shell instance: a BSD/GNU flag that behaves differently on the runner, a pipeline whose count is lost in a subshell, a gate that cannot read its own pattern and reports clean, a sort whose order depends on the locale. An audit of 2026-09-15 classified 223 units: scripts/ci is 44 files and 6,017 lines, the other scripts and bin 82 files and 14,860 lines, lib 45 files and 19,513 lines, and 216 shell test cases 30,872 lines. By disposition 97 are domain logic that belongs in core Rust, 32 orchestration, 34 glue, 3 dead, 14 generated and 43 platform adaptors. A user of the tool needs Bash to run any of it, and Perl reaches the tree through shasum on macOS.
milestones.outcome: A capability may be scripted (ADR 0069): a Rhai script inside the Rust executable orchestrates typed capabilities through the one registry, reaches every surface by the projections that already exist, runs in a sandbox with a declared and enforced effect ceiling, and shell shrinks by migration under a gate that refuses new shell without a declared exemption.

milestones.title: One capability graph, two projections, and no second inventory of what this repository can do
milestones.problem: The executable already declares a capability once and projects it into MCP, HTTP, OpenAPI, Swagger, the command line and now the Cockpit (ADR 2, ADR 4, ADR 12). Everything the repository knows that is not a capability is outside that model: the skills, the rules, the decisions, the documents, the use cases, the examples, the benchmarks and the deployment are each authoritative in their own directory and related to the capabilities only in the reader's head. The Cockpit, the landing page, the navigation, the site indexes and the search each therefore assemble their own view of what exists, and every new subsystem costs an edit in each of them. The failure this produces is not visual: a capability with no documentation, no test and no enforcement looks exactly like one that has all three, because nothing resolves the relation.
milestones.outcome: One typed, deterministic capability graph composes the registries that already own their facts — it does not replace them — and adds typed relations between them that are inferred where a stable convention exists and declared where it does not. Both the running server and the published site render from that one graph: the static projection is the snapshot, the runtime projection is the snapshot plus live state. Navigation, overview, detail, search, the relation view and the coverage matrix are all derived, a dangling relation fails generation rather than rendering as a missing section, and a capability that exists with no documentation, no test or no enforcement is visible as such rather than indistinguishable from one that has them.
milestones.current_state: The Cockpit is a projection of the registry and the index with its own graph derivation (ADR 12, feature/ai-artifacts). Web surfaces are being made discoverable from their producers (ADR 13, in flight). Skills, rules, decisions, use cases, documents, benchmarks and — after the deployment milestone — deployments are each indexed as kinds, and none of them is related to a capability by anything a machine reads.
milestones.desired_state: A contributor registers a capability in the subsystem that owns it, runs generation, and the Cockpit, the navigation, the search, the graph, the documentation index, the coverage matrix, the static snapshot and the runtime metadata all change. Nothing else has to be edited, and CI refuses a change that leaves any of them stale.
non_scope: A hand-maintained menu, page list or capability inventory in any format, including a YAML one
Replacing any registry that is already authoritative for what it owns
A client-side application framework; the Cockpit stays server-rendered with progressive enhancement
A layout description language with coordinates, columns or component trees as data
An external search service for a graph this size
Mutating controls in the Cockpit beyond what the existing authorisation architecture already makes safe
acceptance_criteria: The graph composes the existing authoritative registries and introduces no second store of what they own
Every node has a stable identity that survives a title change, identities are unique, and generation is deterministic over identical inputs
Relations are typed, inferred only from stable conventions, and a relation that does not resolve fails generation with a message naming both ends
The static and the runtime projections come from the same graph, and their representations are equal once runtime-only fields are removed
A surface that requires a running backend is not offered as usable in the static projection, and that decision comes from availability metadata rather than from any check on the page's location
Navigation, overview, detail, search and the coverage matrix are all derived, and adding a capability requires no edit to any of them
The coverage matrix reports documentation, tests, enforcement and benchmarks only where an artifact or a resolved relation supports the claim
The Cockpit is usable on a narrow phone viewport and its core information is present before JavaScript runs
Each enforcement rule introduced here has a check that CI executes, proved by a negative test
risks: Composing eight registries into one model invites a ninth store that holds the composition. The aggregate is derived on every build and committed only as a generated artifact; anything hand-edited in it is a defect.
Inference from names is fragile the day two subsystems name something the same way. Inference is allowed only over stable identities, and ambiguity is an explicit declaration rather than a heuristic.
A coverage matrix that reports what metadata claims rather than what exists is worse than no matrix, because it looks like evidence. Every green cell must resolve to an artifact.
The Cockpit and the web surfaces are being built on other branches right now. This milestone extends them and must land after them rather than beside them.
A graph view is the part everyone wants to build first and the part that matters least if the model underneath is wrong. The model comes first, and the visualisation reads it.

milestones.title: A committed derivation describes something it can be a projection of
milestones.problem: A derived artifact is committed with a fingerprint of what produced it, and the gates compare that fingerprint with the tree. Two things make the recording unable to stay true. It hashes the whole input set, so an unrelated change landing on the trunk invalidates a derivation that is not wrong - the tree simply moved; and where it hashes HEAD, a file inside a commit cannot describe the commit it is in, which apps/majordomus-cli/src/release/changelog.rs:75 states in its own comment while the gate reaches past it. The costs are paid daily and separately: every branch re-derives after every merge, six to thirty-five minutes each time; a fixture without history cannot evaluate the artifact at all; and the refusal that catches a stale recording lives in a pre-commit hook, which cannot run for a merge the server creates. So the first thing in the pipeline that can say no is the publication.
milestones.outcome: A committed derived artifact is a projection of inputs the commit owns. Landing an unrelated change on the trunk does not invalidate it, a fixture whose object database has no history can still evaluate it, and the staleness refusal exists on the path merges actually take - so the first thing that says no is a check rather than the published site.
milestones.current_state: Measured on 2026-09-10. master 3fb515f5c records source_hash e6abaa4665163bcd while its tree hashes to 4fe657a09b10, and three consecutive master Pages runs failed identically at the build step on that refusal; the site last answered from 5e67318db. Two of those three merges were committed by GitHub, where no pre-commit hook exists, and gh api branches/master/protection returns 404 Branch not protected, so the site gate that does check currency is advisory and reports after the merge. c44c2d4c8 and 2ce8d66e5 record the same source_hash as each other - the merge driver resolves derived artifacts to ours, so a stale recording rides through a merge untouched. test/cases/56_derived_current_gate.sh exports git archive HEAD into a fixture with no commits, so the changelog composition reports fatal: Not a valid commit name. One branch paid 185s, 1125s and 2135s of re-derivation in one evening, entirely because the trunk moved underneath it.
milestones.desired_state: The recording covers what the commit owns. The gate that refuses a stale one runs where merges happen. The changelog composes from something a fixture can evaluate. Nobody re-derives to answer a question the derivation was already right about.
non_scope: Making the Pages build re-derive instead of refusing. The input fingerprint is deterministic - three runs on one tree are byte-identical - but the generated content is machine-dependent: %h abbreviates against the local object store, a depth-1 checkout writes a degraded changelog, a concurrent derive can read a sibling worktree root. A build that re-derived could produce a third answer matching neither side. Recorded here because this exit will be proposed again, and because an objection stated as non-determinism of the fingerprint is refutable in one command and would take the correct objection down with it.
Turning on branch protection, or choosing which check is required. A repository setting, and the operator's decision.
Weakening the derived merge driver. Resolving to ours is correct; what is missing is the refusal downstream of it on the server-side path.
acceptance_criteria: A derived artifact committed at one commit is still current at that commit after an unrelated change lands on the trunk
A fixture whose object database does not contain the commit under test can evaluate every derived artifact
The staleness refusal runs on the path a server-side merge takes, or the record names the decision taken instead
No document claims a guard that a merge created by GitHub cannot reach
risks: Narrowing what the recording covers is silent in the dangerous direction: too narrow and staleness stops being detectable, which reads as green rather than as noise. Every change here needs a case that proves the gate still refuses something.
The subsystem is touched by every branch, so a change lands into constant contention with whatever else is deriving.

milestones.title: The runtime has a development surface
milestones.problem: The Cockpit is a faithful projection of a registry that has almost nothing development-shaped in it. Re-measured on today's master, the registry declares exactly three capabilities of kind `command` — executions.start, executions.cancel, peers.announce — and the OpenAPI document the server serves has exactly those three non-GET operations to match. Every command of the development lifecycle lives in a second program, bin/majordomus, and every one of its nodes in the command graph is withheld from every machine surface. So no development surface can be built by adding pages: there is nothing behind the pages to call, and `majordomus_plan_done` answers `unknown tool` because there is no capability for a plan transition. docs/COCKPIT_IDE_AUDIT.md is the evidence; ADR 0040 is the decision it argues for. Until this milestone existed, none of it was in the plan at all: a keyword search of the issues and milestones for palette, diff view, CI status and syntax highlighting returned nothing, so the work could not be scheduled, blocked or reported.
milestones.outcome: A development transition is decided in exactly one place — a `capability!` of kind `command` in the Rust registry — and every surface that offers it is a projection: the CLI, the MCP tool, the HTTP route, the OpenAPI operation and the Cockpit's generated runner form, none of them written by hand. The lifecycle stops being a second program with no surfaces, and the execution history a development surface would show exists somewhere durable.
milestones.current_state: Three command capabilities, all of them about executions or peers. The lifecycle transitions exist only in lib/plan.sh and lib/start.sh. `majordomus run` executes in its own process and never reaches the running server, so the execution plane the Cockpit shows and the one a person uses are disjoint. A server whose executable has been replaced still reports itself `ready`. Two capabilities — devtask.issue and devtask.milestone — landed after the audit's base and give the runtime its first canonical read of an issue and a milestone as work; neither of them writes anything.
milestones.desired_state: Phase A of the audit's plan has landed end to end — one transition, one capability, four surfaces, no hand-written projection — and the phases that depend on it are schedulable against it. The three load-bearing defects named in the audit's F-table are fixed or explicitly deferred with a record, rather than carried silently under every later measurement.
non_scope: A terminal, a PTY or shell execution on any surface. The audit records this as a non-goal and share/cockpit/palette.js already states the boundary in terms.
Editing repository source in the browser. The Cockpit refuses every non-GET route by decision, and this milestone does not reopen that decision.
Retries and a scheduler. apps/majordomus-cli/src/execution/mod.rs states in its own module documentation that it has none, by decision.
A second datastore or a second project model. The records stay canonical and the runtime reads them.
The `/cockpit/worktrees` response time. It is F3 in the audit's table and is being fixed on fix/cockpit-answers-quickly; this milestone references that work rather than duplicating it.
A wholesale port of lib/*.sh. Phase A is one transition; the rest is scheduled behind it or not at all.
acceptance_criteria: The registry declares at least one capability of kind command that changes a development record, and the generated OpenAPI carries its non-GET operation without anyone editing the document
The same transition is reachable from the CLI, from MCP and over HTTP, and the Cockpit's existing generic runner drives it with no Cockpit source edited
An execution a person starts is visible to the server that serves the repository, or the record says which decision was taken instead and why
A surface that reports a runtime as ready cannot be serving an executable that no longer exists on disk
No claim in docs/COCKPIT_IDE_AUDIT.md is left standing that a command in this repository contradicts
risks: Phase A is the whole architecture in miniature. If the pattern does not land cleanly on one transition, no later phase would have worked either, and the correct response is to stop rather than to widen.

A second name for an existing concept can land in parallel. One already has: the devtask module documents itself as a join over plan and trace rather than a second model, and holds an equality assertion against plan.issues. It is additive and should stay, but its readiness vocabulary refines the canonical statuses, and Phase A should converge the naming rather than grow a third.
Master moves during the work. It moved eleven times during the audit that produced this milestone, and again between that audit and this record.

milestones.title: Every LLM session joins the Majordomus mesh at start, told the mesh as work
milestones.problem: Mesh participation was left to the worker: the start printed one health line (lib/capture.sh mj_capture_mesh_line), MCP initialize instructions never mentioned the mesh (apps/majordomus-cli/src/mcp/protocol.rs), only Claude Code had a lifecycle adapter (lib/capture.sh MJ_CAPTURE_LIFECYCLE), nothing surfaced handovers or reviews waiting for this machine, and no gate noticed a task built outside the mesh. Survey of 2026-10-10 at master a804ae2045.
milestones.outcome: Any LLM session that starts in a repository with an enabled mesh is on the mesh from its first turn, told who works where on every machine and what waits for it, and a task built outside the mesh is refused by the repository's gates.
milestones.current_state: Partly automatic: an announcing MCP client is projected as a mesh session with advisory claims; everything else is the worker's memory.
milestones.desired_state: mesh.briefing at every start and MCP initialize, a mesh session and a claim for every task, a gated rule, projections and the Cockpit, an article.
non_scope: Changing what the mesh may decide: it stays observation, not authority (ADR 0050).
acceptance_criteria: A runtime's briefing shows another machine's live session, its exclusive claim, its handover and its review
The start briefing of a checkout whose mesh runs carries the briefing lines
An MCP initialize answer on a server whose mesh runs names the briefing and the protocol
After majordomus start the task's scope is a live claim on every linked runtime
finish refuses a task whose scope was never claimed while the mesh was enabled
A Codex or Gemini session start runs the same lifecycle, proved against the real tool
The provider projections and README name mesh.briefing and the protocol
The article is published by the site build and passes site-check
A client that starts the MCP server from a checkout with no executable it can build is served by the installed release and told so (ADR 0172)
A bare session start in a checkout is handed the session-start prompt, so the worker joins the board and takes up the active task without being asked (ADR 0172)
risks: A start that waits on the mesh is a slower start for everyone: the briefing is read within a budget and skipped, not waited for.

milestones.title: Everything that happens in the repository is followed in one stream
milestones.problem: A worker that wants to know what is happening around it reads six surfaces with six cursors: the mesh journal (where about 95% of events are identical session re-projections on every heartbeat), the board, the executor trail, the executions, and GitHub's pull requests and checks through gh. Nothing joins them, nothing says which of it is addressed to the reader, and every session that needs it hand-rolls a jq loop over majordomus mesh events and gh pr list. Sessions miss reviews and handovers addressed to them for hours because nothing they read shows them.
milestones.outcome: majordomus monitor is the one stream: a typed, cursor-paged feed of signals from every source, with the heartbeat noise folded away and what is addressed to the reader marked and listed first, served by the running server over HTTP, MCP and the command line (with --follow), shown live in the Cockpit, printed at every session start, named by the provider bootstrap, documented and released.
milestones.current_state: No monitor command, module or capability exists (origin/master 890e112d04, 0.20.0). mesh.events, peers, integration.events and executions.events each answer their own page; the CLI renders mesh events one by one, unfiltered.
milestones.desired_state: One read capability, monitor, answers a page of signals after an opaque cursor across mesh, board, executor and executions (and GitHub when reachable, as a reported source state otherwise); majordomus monitor --follow streams it; /cockpit/monitor shows it live; the start briefing and majordomus context say what happened since the last look.
non_scope: Writing anything: the monitor reads; acting on a signal stays with the capability that owns the act
A second journal or event store: every signal is derived from a source that already records it
Push notifications to systems outside the repository (Slack, mail); a notifier subscribes to the stream later
acceptance_criteria: One capability answers a page of signals from mesh, board, executor trail and executions after an opaque cursor, and the next page after the answer's cursor repeats nothing
A session_opened that only re-projects an unchanged session is counted as suppressed and never shown; a new session or a changed intent is shown
Signals addressed to the reader are marked for_you and listed first in a briefing
majordomus monitor --follow streams new signals and --count/--until let a script wait for one and exit
An unreachable source is reported with its reason, never answered as empty
The Cockpit shows the stream live, and the start briefing and majordomus context print what happened since the last look
The provider bootstrap names the command; docs/MONITOR.md, the README and a blog article describe it; the release carries it
risks: A stream that shows everything is as unread as six that show their own: the fold and for_you are the feature, not the joining.
GitHub is network: it must never make a local page slow or an absent network look like a quiet repository.

milestones.problem: The operator holds work in vendor-hosted workspaces — a ChatGPT Project first, others after — and has no machine access to it. Whatever is decided there is invisible to every instrument this repository has: it cannot be searched, cited, carried into a handover, or linked to the decision it produced. The obvious repair is the wrong one twice over. Scraping a page produces a corpus with no identity, no provenance and no way to tell a change from a re-render; and building the corpus into the layer the way tracked content is built would publish, on a public website, a body of private conversation the vendor holds under an authenticated session. ADR 0025 settles the shape: the catalogue of workspaces is the repository's own statement and is tracked; the content is this checkout's state and is not.
milestones.outcome: A workspace is a declared object of the layer — vendor, identity, what the operator authorised, which browser profile reaches it, which capabilities it is expected to have — and rides the existing kind pipeline onto every surface with no code that special-cases it. Its content is synced by the Node tooling layer that already drives the system browser, lands under `.ai/local/workspaces/`, carries provenance and a support level on every record, and is read back through exactly one capability shaped like `continuity`: served, never published. A sync is incremental from a durable checkpoint, idempotent on replay, fails closed when an observed contract breaks, and never writes a credential anywhere.
milestones.current_state: Nothing exists. There is no workspace kind, no adapter, no store, no capability and no gate. The repository does drive a browser — Playwright over the system Chrome, in `scripts/lib/ui-audit.mjs` and `scripts/lib/cockpit-probe.mjs`, wired into CI and skipping cleanly where Chrome is absent — and it has no convention at all for holding a credential, only a negative one that fails the site build when a secret-shaped string reaches rendered output.
milestones.desired_state: `majordomus workspaces` lists what is declared and what is synced, with the age and the support level of each. A sync is one command in the tooling layer, resumable, bounded, and provable from sanitised fixtures in CI without touching a live account. Adding a second vendor means writing an adapter and a declaration, not editing every consumer. Nothing under `.ai/local/workspaces/` reaches the website, the generated documentation, or any published projection, and a gate proves it rather than a sentence promising it.
non_scope: Any write to the vendor — no message is sent, no file is uploaded, no conversation is renamed
Any dependency added to majordomus-cli; the boundary of ADR 0025 is the point
Any credential, cookie, token or authorisation header stored anywhere in the tree or the state directory
Any bypass of authentication, multi-factor prompts, rate limits or anti-abuse controls
Publishing synced content to the website or any public projection
A second vendor adapter before the first one is proven
acceptance_criteria: A workspace declaration is a tracked object of a declared kind, closed by an allow file, described by a schema, and reaches the object surface with no code that special-cases it

Every synced record carries its upstream identity, a local identity that does not depend on a title, a content hash, the transport that produced it and a support level, all as typed fields rather than prose
The store under .ai/local/workspaces/ has a declared layout, a checkpoint, a retention cap in policy and a doctor stanza that measures it
A sync resumes from its checkpoint, produces the same store when replayed, and marks a record removed upstream rather than deleting it silently
An observed contract that breaks fails closed and falls back to the browser transport; no partial parse is ever persisted
CI proves the mapper and the sync from sanitised fixtures, with no live account and no network
No credential reaches the repository, the state directory, a fixture, a log or a snapshot, and a gate greps for it
A gate fails if majordomus-cli gains a dependency, and a gate fails if any published projection reaches .ai/local/workspaces/
The subsystem is documented in docs/ and every rule it states is enforced by a check CI executes
risks: The vendor's private surface is not a contract and will change without notice. Anything that treats an observed shape as canonical will break loudly and, worse, silently. The observed shape is a transport detail with a fingerprint and a compatibility state; the canonical model is this repository's.

A synced corpus is the largest body of text this repository has ever held and the only one it did not write. Every mechanism that walks files must be told about it explicitly, because none of them will notice it on their own.
The distance between reading one's own authorised workspace and automating a vendor's site is a policy, not a technicality. The declaration names what was authorised; the adapter never exceeds it.
The tooling layer is a devDependency of this checkout, not part of the released tool. A feature that only works where node_modules is installed must say so rather than appear broken.

milestones.title: Every failure the runtime can suffer is bounded, tested or stated, and changes the health it reports
milestones.problem: Readiness stays true for a degraded index and knows nothing of a lost lease or the mesh (apps/majordomus-cli/src/capability/builtin/health.rs:214; was_lost reaches only GET / at apps/majordomus-cli/src/http/router.rs:710); health.report has no mesh dimension (apps/majordomus-cli/src/capability/builtin/health.rs:299); 'degraded' has three unrelated meanings. The HTTP server reads request bodies with no deadline on four workers (apps/majordomus-cli/src/http/server.rs:23,208-222), so four slow clients hold the server. Of the failure classes the pack names, the audit found tests for SIGKILL, port collision, an unwritable lease directory and a frozen owner, and none for disk full, a read-only journal directory, a slow client, a frozen worker or a kill between lease creation and its first write; lease keep-alive write errors are swallowed (apps/majordomus-cli/src/lease.rs:1058-1060). The pack's premise of structured logging is refuted: logging is human tracing fmt on stderr with no JSON, correlation id or redaction (apps/majordomus-cli/src/logging.rs:29-37). The top-level doctor is a governance doctor (lib/doctor.sh:53-77). Measured in the runtime baseline audit of 2026-10-09 at master 1fb8d6be44 (plan/RUNTIME_BASELINE.md).
milestones.outcome: A client can tell running from ready from mesh-healthy from degraded on one endpoint; no client can hold a worker past a declared deadline; each failure class in a published table names its test or its stated limitation.
milestones.current_state: Implemented: /api/v1/live, the lease's client-side bounded waits, link timeouts, clock-skew bounds, the mesh doctor's typed checks (apps/majordomus-cli/src/mesh/doctor.rs:93-372). Partial: readiness, health, failure-class coverage. Absent: server-side request deadlines.
milestones.desired_state: The failure table in docs/DEVELOPMENT_RUNTIME.md has no row without a test or a limitation, a case refuses a row with neither, and readiness and health reflect every state the runtime already knows about itself.
non_scope: Circuit breakers; the audit found no evidence one is justified.
A metrics stack or log shipping; the runtime reports through its own capabilities.
Journal durability, which is I2137 (mesh-journal-converges).
acceptance_criteria: /api/v1/ready reports false with a named reason after a lease loss
health.report carries a mesh check when the mesh is enabled
Slow clients hold no worker past the declared deadline
Every failure class in the published table names a CI test or a stated limitation
validation: cargo test --test health_server --test http_serve --test mcp_shared --test lease_busy
MJ_TEST_JOBS=4 bash test/run.sh <the cases these issues add>
risks: Making readiness stricter can make deploy health checks fail where they passed; the fly-deployment health block reads /api/v1/live and must keep doing so.
A deadline on request reads that is too short breaks slow links; it must be declared and measured.

milestones.title: The container image is a projection of the repository model, and its smoke is its evidence
milestones.problem: Majordomus has no deployment at all: no container, no hosting provider, no way for anyone who is not standing in front of this checkout to see the layer it serves. The obvious repair is the wrong one. A Dockerfile and a fly.toml written by hand would be a second description of facts the repository already holds — the port the server binds, the routes it registers, the assets the site build produces, the binary the workspace names — and every one of those pairs would drift the first time one half changed. The repository already refuses that shape everywhere else: capabilities are declared once and projected into CLI, HTTP, MCP, OpenAPI, docs and the site, and generate --check fails when a projection is stale. A deployment must arrive the same way or not at all.
milestones.outcome: One canonical deployment object under .ai/repo/deployments/ describes the image; a typed Rust model parses and validates it; the Dockerfile, its ignore file, the GHCR image that docker-image.yml and release.yml build, its smoke derived from the route registry, the doctor checks, the documentation and the cockpit view are projections of that object and of the capability registry, each checked for drift. The published image runs as a non-root user, carries no secret and no developer path, answers live and ready in its smoke, and has measured size, cold-start and memory baselines. Re-scoped 2026-10-14 from a Fly.io deployment, which the owner disconnected on 2026-10-12.
milestones.current_state: Measured 2026-10-14 on master e28daccd9b: .ai/repo/deployments/majordomus.yaml is the canonical object; deploy/Dockerfile and its ignore file are generated from it (Alpine, uid 10001, exec-form entrypoint); docker-image.yml builds and smoke-tests the image on pull requests and on master, and release.yml publishes it to GHCR; .github/actions/image-smoke checks the image runs as non-root and answers /api/v1/live and /api/v1/ready; deploy.list, deploy.get, deploy.check and deploy.observed are capabilities. Missing: a smoke derived from the route registry, a secret and developer-path scan of the image, an SBOM, size, cold-start and memory baselines, a documentation page. The object still carries region, machines and resources, which nothing reads since Fly.io was disconnected on 2026-10-12.
milestones.desired_state: The GHCR image is a projection of the canonical object like every other artifact: generated, checked for drift, smoke-tested from the route registry, scanned for secrets and developer paths, measured against recorded budgets, documented and shown in the cockpit. Whether region, machines and resources leave the deployment/v1 schema is decided and recorded.
non_scope: Any dependency, in code, script, documentation, CI or default, on ~/dev/prismatic-platform
A provider abstraction covering hosts other than the one this repository deploys to
Kubernetes, Nomad, buildpacks, Nixpacks or a second container implementation
A persistent volume, a database or any stateful service, unless a measured requirement forces one
Mutating deployment operations exposed to unauthenticated HTTP or to the browser
Profile-guided optimisation
acceptance_criteria: One canonical deployment object is the only place the port, the region, the resources, the Machine count, the health routes, the build inputs and the budgets are stated
Every image artifact — the Dockerfile and its ignore file — is generated, marked as generated with its source and its regeneration command, and fails generate --check when edited by hand
The deployment reads are declared once in the capability registry and appear in the CLI, the HTTP API, MCP, OpenAPI and the generated documentation without a second registration
The smoke suite is derived from the route registry; no second list of endpoints exists anywhere
The production image runs as a non-root user, contains no build toolchain, no repository history, no secret and no absolute developer path
The published image answers live and ready in its smoke, run from outside the container on a free host port
Image size, binary size, build context size, cold start, resident memory and endpoint latency are measured, recorded as baselines and gated against unexplained regression
No credential is written to the repository, to a Docker layer, to a generated file, to the site or to a log, and the image is published with the workflow's own token
Every rule this milestone states is enforced by a check that CI executes
risks: Generation can hide the Dockerfile from the people who must read it. The generated file has to stay idiomatic and reviewable; the source describes intent, the output describes mechanics, and a contributor who edits the output is told which file to change instead.

The route topology and the served surfaces are being rewritten on other branches under ADR 0013. A smoke suite pinned to today's paths would be stale on arrival, so it must read the route registry rather than a path list.
256 MB is a hypothesis. It is held only as long as a measured run under that limit passes; the evidence, not the preference, decides the final number.
A deployment touches money. The first deploy must not leave two Machines running, and the Machine inventory is asserted rather than assumed.

The bootstrap credential comes from outside this repository. It may be used to obtain an authenticated session and nowhere else; anything else would make Majordomus depend on Prismatic Platform, which is forbidden.

milestones.title: A supervisory control layer that is real rather than described
milestones.problem: An AI worker in a repository has no durable memory, no declared scope, and no contract that says when its work is finished. Every session starts from nothing and ends by asserting success. The evidence that a rule is enforced is usually a sentence claiming it is.
milestones.outcome: A repository carries one policy, a small set of profiles, durable task state, and a set of commands that refuse work which does not meet a declared contract — with every rule dispatched from a registry that proves it reaches the command claiming to run it.
milestones.current_state: Delivered. The policy, the profiles, the durable records, the command surface, the doctrine registry with wiring reconciliation and the provider projections all exist and are covered by the behavioural suite.
milestones.desired_state: Unchanged: this milestone is the base every later one is measured against.
non_scope: Measuring tokens or cost
Constraining a provider's runtime
acceptance_criteria: One canonical policy projects to every provider and drift is detectable in one command
A task declares scope, and work outside it is reported
A finish contract is evaluated rather than asserted
Every enforced rule is declared in a registry, dispatched from it, and proven to reach its command
Every behaviour has a case in the suite and CI runs it
risks: The floor is bash 3.2 and BSD userland, which bounds what the engine can be asked to do.

evidence.result: the behavioural suite covering the policy, the profiles, the task lifecycle, the doctrine registry and the provider projections passes

milestones.title: A task is bound to the intent it serves
milestones.problem: The intent engine can say which intent an issue or a set of paths serves (intent preflight), and nothing asks it. `start` takes a description and a scope; the task record names no issue and no intent; the context a worker is handed says nothing of the criteria the work is for; a handover carries a commit and no trace of the intent it was written under. Work under an intent whose plan was never critiqued is found by `intent validate` after it began, not refused before.
milestones.outcome: `start` names an issue, an intent or a declared exemption, asks the binding capability what the task serves, and refuses a refused binding where the policy requires binding. The task record carries what was named and the revision it resolved at. `context` briefs the worker from the binding, `handover` pins the revision, and `handover --resolve` reports drift.
milestones.current_state: intents.preflight exists with no caller. The task record has no issue, intent or exemption field. No exemption class exists anywhere. Nothing computes a revision of an intent, its plan or its critique.
milestones.desired_state: One derivation, `Intents::binding`, answered by `intents.binding` on every surface and asked by start, context and handover.
non_scope: Refusing a finish on unmet criteria
Producing or executing a critique
Moving the task lifecycle from shell to Rust (ADR 0047)
acceptance_criteria: A task started with --issue, --intent or by scope resolves through intents.binding, and an ambiguous or refused binding does not start where the policy requires binding
An exemption is a policy-declared class with a reason, recorded in the task record and the ledger
The context of a bound task carries the intent section, from the binding
A handover carries the binding revision and --resolve reports drift
The command line, HTTP and MCP answer the same binding
risks: The records, the ADR and the tests they name land in one change: a criterion whose evidence reference does not resolve fails intent validate, so no part of this milestone reaches the trunk without the rest.

Requiring binding in this repository refuses the scope-only `start` every session uses today; the refusal must name the three ways through (an issue, an intent, an exemption) or it reads as the tool being broken.
A pin stored in a task is one step from stored intent state; it must stay a hash compared on read and never a stage or a verdict (rule project.an-intent-outlives-its-sessions).

milestones.title: Work is traceable to the intent it serves, and an intent is satisfied only by evidence
milestones.problem: This repository models the work: milestones are outcomes, issues are execution contracts, commits trace to issues and claims trace to recorded runs. Nothing above the milestone records what must become true for a person, so no command can say which outcome a change serves, whether a set of finished milestones achieved what they were for, or which intents have no work and which work has no intent. The public site stated as much: 'There is no intent object, no intent registry and no intent id.' An intent lived only in a prompt, and a prompt is unversioned, unenforced and gone when the session ends.
milestones.outcome: An intent is a typed record above the milestones that realise it: a statement, its invariants, and satisfaction criteria each naming the evidence that settles it. Its stage is derived from the plan's milestone status and its satisfaction from the evidence ledger, never stored. A gate refuses an intent that names no milestone or evidence that resolves to nothing, a session's preflight names the intent its work serves or refuses, the Cockpit shows intents with measured and enforced coverage of its scripts, and a milestone closes on GitHub only when the intents it serves are satisfied.
milestones.current_state: Milestones and issues are validated by `majordomus plan validate`; claims are joined to recorded runs by `majordomus evidence`. There is no intent kind, no intent capability and no gate that relates work to an intent.
milestones.desired_state: A worker asks which intent a change serves and one capability answers from the plan, or refuses naming the missing link. A reader asks whether an intent is satisfied and the answer is derived from recorded evidence, not from a merged pull request.
non_scope: A second task lifecycle beside the plan; the stage is derived and nothing transitions
Storing an intent status, or stamping an intent from a merge
Deriving a plan from an intent automatically
acceptance_criteria: Slice 1 — typed record and gate: the intent kind, its schema in the distribution and the skeleton, the read-only capabilities intents.list, intents.record, intents.validate and intents.preflight on every surface, and the intent-check gate refusing an invalid intent model

Slice 2 — satisfaction is decided by evidence alone (ADR 0107): completion discharges obligations and never decides whether an intent is satisfied; the intent engine is the one authority for a criterion's verdict, and a derived `verdict` answers satisfaction separately from the plan-derived stage
Slice 3 — preflight join: devcontext and the session start name the intent the task serves, from intents.preflight, and load its governance
Slice 4 — Cockpit Intent view, with the Cockpit's JavaScript coverage measured and enforced by a gate
Slice 5 — GitHub reconciliation: milestones projected with the intent they serve, and a closure gate that refuses to close a milestone whose intents are unsatisfied
risks: An intent model that grows a status or a transition becomes a second lifecycle beside the plan, and the two would disagree the first time an issue is re-planned.

Satisfaction criteria backed by commands or deployments are not derivable from the ledger yet, so an intent resting only on them can never read satisfied; its verdict reads unknown until those kinds become derivable.

milestones.title: The plan of an intent is held to it before execution
milestones.problem: An intent (ADR 0070) names its milestones and the evidence that settles each criterion, but nothing relates a criterion to the work meant to make it true. An intent can name a milestone whose issues address two of its four criteria and nothing says the other two have no work until verification finds them unmet. Planning starts from a prompt: what a worker observed was missing, and what a review of the plan overlooked, live in a terminal scroll and are gone when the session ends.
milestones.outcome: An issue names the intent criteria it serves; coverage of every criterion is derived from the plan and refused when a criterion has no work or work has no purpose. The gap a worker observed and the critique of the plan are typed records validated against the intent and the plan, and work does not start on an intent whose plan was never critiqued or has an open blocking finding.
milestones.current_state: Issues carry objective, why and acceptance criteria but no link to an intent criterion. No gap or critique record kind exists. plan validate checks dependencies, waves, cycles and scope overlap within the plan only.
milestones.desired_state: intent validate reports the coverage of every criterion, the purpose of every issue, and the findings of the gap and critique records, and exits non-zero when the plan does not carry the intent.
non_scope: Deriving issues from a gap automatically
Judging whether a criterion is met

milestones.title: Every MCP transport delivers each request at most once, bounds what it carries, and honours cancellation
milestones.problem: The MCP projection is already one registry walk: tools and resources come from apps/majordomus-cli/src/mcp/surface.rs:367-394, annotations from the declared effect (apps/majordomus-cli/src/mcp/protocol.rs:446-456), held by apps/majordomus-cli/tests/projections.rs:26, apps/majordomus-cli/tests/mcp_conformance.rs and case 940. The pack's premise that MCP keeps independent lists is refuted. The transport is the defect. The stdio bridge resends the same tools/call after a 60 s timeout or any 4xx other than 404 (apps/majordomus-cli/src/mcp/bridge.rs:25,352; apps/majordomus-cli/src/commands/mcp.rs:283,301), so a slow writer can run twice. notifications/cancelled is dropped (apps/majordomus-cli/src/mcp/protocol.rs:234-238) and could not be forwarded anyway because the bridge is sequential under a mutex (apps/majordomus-cli/src/commands/mcp.rs:218). stdin lines and bridge responses are unbounded (apps/majordomus-cli/src/mcp/stdio.rs:40, apps/majordomus-cli/src/mcp/bridge.rs:85); the Streamable HTTP endpoint ignores MCP-Protocol-Version, issues predictable session ids (apps/majordomus-cli/src/http/mcp.rs:159) and can reap a session whose request is still running (apps/majordomus-cli/src/http/mcp.rs:138). The provider launch configurations are hand-written and diagnosed by substring (apps/majordomus-cli/src/capability/builtin/mcp.rs:394-399). Measured in the runtime baseline audit of 2026-10-09 at master 1fb8d6be44 (plan/RUNTIME_BASELINE.md).
milestones.outcome: A client gets each answer once or is told the outcome is unknown, can cancel what it started, cannot exhaust the server with one message, and finds its launch configuration generated from the provider declaration and diagnosed by parsing it.
milestones.current_state: Implemented and tested: stdout hygiene (apps/majordomus-cli/tests/mcp_stdio.rs), malformed traffic (apps/majordomus-cli/tests/mcp_conformance.rs::malformed_traffic_is_answered_and_the_session_survives), session isolation over HTTP (apps/majordomus-cli/tests/mcp_conformance_http.rs), protocol negotiation (apps/majordomus-cli/src/mcp/protocol.rs:71). Absent: idempotency on resend, cancellation, symmetric bounds, the version header, generated client configs. Authorization of writers and the effect laundering through executions.start for remote callers are I2123 (runtime-trust).
milestones.desired_state: The audit's MCP rows are all I in plan/RUNTIME_BASELINE.md, each with a real-process test: a timed-out writer runs once, a cancelled call stops, an oversized message is refused with its real cause, a long request is not reaped, a Codex config without its table is reported unwired.
non_scope: A GET/SSE stream on the Streamable HTTP endpoint; docs/MCP.md documents its absence and no client here needs it.
Authorization and remote callers, which are I2123.
A second tool list or MCP-specific capability metadata; the registry stays the one source.
acceptance_criteria: A mutating tool call that outlasts the bridge timeout is executed exactly once
notifications/cancelled stops a running call within a bound
One declared message bound applies to stdin, request bodies and bridge responses, each with a test one byte over it
The three client launch configurations are generated and their diagnosis parses them

Answering 'outcome unknown' instead of resending moves a decision to the client; the error text must say what to check.

milestones.title: The cooperation journal is durable, converges under any delivery order, and never lets a stale claim win
milestones.problem: The signed journal's grammar and fold are sound where tested: events are signed over canonical JSON (apps/majordomus-cli/src/mesh/journal.rs:934-948), the fold orders by (lamport, stream, seq) (apps/majordomus-cli/src/mesh/state.rs:508-513), and proptests permute deliveries. Its durability and its claims are not. Journal::persist ignores write errors (apps/majordomus-cli/src/mesh/journal.rs:1984), never fsyncs, and reload drops unparsable lines silently (apps/majordomus-cli/src/mesh/journal.rs:1407-1413); an append after a torn tail fuses the next event into the corrupt line. Claims have no fencing: expiry is a fold-time verdict that reverses when the same stream beats again after a sleep or partition (apps/majordomus-cli/src/mesh/journal.rs:1681-1697, apps/majordomus-cli/src/mesh/state.rs:656-661), and the revived claim then beats a claim admitted legitimately in its absence. Release is checked per run, not per session (apps/majordomus-cli/src/mesh/cooperation.rs:3373-3390). The sync budget ignores the size of the marks (apps/majordomus-cli/src/mesh/journal.rs:1734-1766), so a busy journal can exceed MAX_LINK_MESSAGE (apps/majordomus-cli/src/mesh/link.rs:67,70). mesh.events paging returns the journal's maximum lamport as the cursor and skips events (apps/majordomus-cli/src/capability/builtin/mesh.rs:594-596, apps/majordomus-cli/src/mesh/journal.rs:2124-2133). docs/MESH.md:189-190 claims permutation testing that covers one stream of six events. Measured in the runtime baseline audit of 2026-10-09 at master 1fb8d6be44 (plan/RUNTIME_BASELINE.md).
milestones.outcome: An event the runtime accepted survives a crash or is reported lost; replicas with the same authenticated event set produce the same digest after any delivery order; a claim that expired never returns to beat a claim admitted while it was gone, and every claim conflict is announced; every page of the journal returns every event once.
milestones.current_state: Durable: the node key and every accepted event, with no fsync and ignored write errors. Memory only: registry, links, nonces, tombstones, beats. Exclusivity is local admission plus deterministic post-hoc naming of the winner, with no fencing token and no notification on Held to Conflicted. The journal reload trust check and the Lamport forward bound are I2124 (milestone runtime-trust, in progress on fix/a-remote-caller-cannot-write) and are not repeated here; runtime-trust's criterion that 'an expired claim does not return as live' is met by I2138 in this milestone.
milestones.desired_state: Every row of the audit's consistency contract (plan/RUNTIME_BASELINE.md) names a test: torn tail, failed write, crash during compaction, revived claim, release by another session, sync at the mark bound, paging across shared lamports, and a randomized multi-stream property test with permutation and duplication. docs/MESH.md states exclusivity as local admission with announced conflicts, not as a lock.
non_scope: A global lock, quorum or coordinator. Pack invariant 5 allows refusing strong guarantees instead; the docs already disclaim linearizability (docs/MESH.md:26-27,612-613) and this milestone keeps that position unless an ADR decides otherwise.
The journal reload trust check and the Lamport bound, which are I2124.
Persisting tombstones, which the docs record as a deliberate limit.
acceptance_criteria: A torn or unreadable journal line is counted and reported by mesh doctor, and no complete event before or after it is lost
A write failure is reported and the event is not acknowledged as stored
A claim that expired and revived after a partition is Conflicted, not Held, against a claim admitted during its absence, on every runtime
Two replicas fed the same authenticated events in any order and with duplicates report equal digests, by a multi-stream property test
No sync message exceeds MAX_LINK_MESSAGE, and mesh.events pages return every event once
risks: Adding an epoch to ClaimAcquired is a wire change; it needs the link or event schema version handled as I2164 prices it, or old runtimes will refuse or misread the new field.
fsync on every append costs latency on the heartbeat path; the bound chosen must be measured, not assumed.
I2124 edits the same reload path in apps/majordomus-cli/src/mesh/journal.rs; I2137 should land after it.

milestones.title: A visitor sees the product prove itself, and can check every claim it makes
milestones.problem: A developer who has never seen Majordomus meets a homepage whose first viewport describes a supervisory control layer in its own vocabulary, beside a console that illustrates each lifecycle command separately. Nothing on it shows the tool doing the one thing that sets it apart — refusing work a worker calls finished — as one story a newcomer can follow, and no page exists that a link from outside could send somebody to. The README's first transcript is hand-written. Underneath, the use-case catalogue reached the site without any scenario since scenarios moved into the body, so every executable use case read as merely described.
milestones.outcome: One recorded scenario tells the whole story — a worker strays, claims it is done, hands over, and is refused until the repository's own test passes — and it drives the homepage hero, its own route, the README's first transcript and the live smoke check, each held to the recorded run by a gate rather than by care.
milestones.current_state: The homepage hero replays the lifecycle command by command; there is no challenge route; README.md's first block is an illustration; scenario steps can only invoke the tool, so no use case shows a file outside the claimed scope being refused; catalogue.json carries no scenario and every use case's maturity is described; scripts/pages verify asks only which commit the public site serves.
milestones.desired_state: A worker step lets a fixture scenario show the change it judges. Fabricated adoption figures, testimonials, logos or benchmark comparisons

/challenge/ and the homepage carry every recorded command and decision line of the run, and nothing else stands in for them

milestones.title: Routing recommendations derived from measured cost
milestones.problem: Choosing which capability to send a task to is currently a judgement nobody can check. A recommendation not derived from measured outcomes is an opinion with a command around it.
milestones.outcome: The profile a task should run under is recommended from measured cost per accepted outcome, and the recommendation names the data it came from.
milestones.current_state: Not started, and gated on cost per accepted outcome existing at all.
milestones.desired_state: A worker can ask which profile a class of task should use and get an answer traceable to measurements.
non_scope: Automatic routing without a person's decision
acceptance_criteria: Every recommendation names the measurements it was derived from
Insufficient data produces no recommendation rather than a weak one
The recommendation is advisory and never silently changes a profile
risks: A recommendation that is followed becomes a cause of the data that justifies it.

milestones.title: Profiles become runtime constraints rather than advice
milestones.problem: A profile declares an effort and a verbosity, and then nothing enforces them. The worker reads the projection and is trusted to behave. An axis that only ever appears in generated prose is a preference, not a control.
milestones.outcome: A profile's axes become opt-in runtime clamps a provider actually applies — read size, output condensation, subagent budget — with the limit derived from the profile rather than configured twice.
milestones.current_state: Not started. The profiles exist and project correctly; nothing derives a runtime limit from them.
milestones.desired_state: Starting a task under a profile constrains what the worker may do, and the constraint is visible in the same place the profile is.
non_scope: Provider-specific behaviour that cannot be verified from this repository
acceptance_criteria: At least one runtime limit is derived from the profile and applied, not merely printed
The limit is opt-in and a repository that does not want it is unaffected
A behavioural case proves the limit changes what happens, not only what is reported
risks: Only providers that expose a real knob can be clamped honestly; the rest would be theatre.
